Algebra

A — Expansion

✦ Multiply each term in the bracket by ALL the other terms in the other bracket.

Example
(x + 5)(x − 6) = x² + 5x − 6x − 30 = x² − x − 30
⚠️ Note: (x − 2)² → (1st term)² + (2 × 1st × 2nd) + (2nd term)² = x² − 4x + 4
B — Factorization
Steps — always check in this order:
  1. 1Always check for Highest Common Factor (HCF)
  2. 2Check if it's a Difference of Two Squares → e.g. 2x² − 8y²
  3. 3Check if it's a Quadratic (Mode 5-3)
Example 1 — HCF
5a + 15ab = 5a(1 + 3b)
Example 2 — Diff of Squares
4c² − 16d² = 4(c² − 4d²) = 4(c−2d)(c+2d)
Example 3 — Quadratic
2x² + 8x − 10 ÷ 2 = x² + 4x − 5 = (x − 1)(x + 5)

ii) Single Fractions

✦ Try to factorize the equations, then see if there are terms that cancel each other.

Example
6x³ + 13x² − 5x4x² − 25
= x(6x² + 13x − 5)(2x−5)(2x+5)
= x(3x−1)(2x+5)(2x−5)(2x+5)
= x(3x − 1)(2x − 5)
iii) Non-Single Fractions
  1. 1Try to factorize if possible
  2. 2Make a common denominator
  3. 3Expand brackets in the numerator only
  4. 4Factorize and simplify
Example
x+1x+2 − x−2x−1
= (x−1)(x+1) − (x−2)(x+2)(x+2)(x−1)
= x²−1 − x²+4(x+2)(x−1)
= 3(x+2)(x−1)
D — Equations

✦ Solve to get the letter (variable) alone on one side.

Example
4(3p + 1) = 15p + 8
12p + 4 = 15p + 8
−3p = 4 → p = −43
✅ Check: Put the value you found back into the original equation to verify!
E — Solving Fractional Equations
Example
9 + 2x4 = 3x + 2
9 + 2x = 4(3x + 2)
9 + 2x = 12x + 8
10x = 1 → x = 110
⚠️ Important Rule

You can only multiply the denominator to the other side if the whole fraction is alone on one side. If there are other terms, move them first!

e.g. 9+2x4 − 2 = 3x + 2 → you must move the 2 first, THEN multiply by 4
Quadratic Equations — 2 Methods

Method 1: Factorize (Mode 5-3)

x² + 6x − 7 = 0
(x − 1)(x + 7) = 0
x = 1 , x = −7

Method 2: Quadratic Formula

x = −b ± √b²−4ac2a
where ax² + bx + c = 0
📝 Note: x² − 16 = 0 for example can be done with Mode 5-3. The term beside x is 0 (no x term), so enter: a=1, b=0, c=−16.
F — Completing the Square
Case 1: No coefficient for x²
Example: x² − 10x + 40
  1. 1Write (x − b/2)² → (x − 10/2)² = (x − 5)²
  2. 2Add the last term beside the bracket → (x−5)² + 40
  3. 3Square the 2nd term in bracket and put it outside with −ve sign → (x−5)² + 40 − 25
  4. 4Simplify → (x − 5)² + 15
Case 2: Coefficient for x²
Example: 3x² − 12x + 7
  1. 1Take the coefficient as a common factor from first 2 terms only → 3(x² − 4x) + 7
  2. 2Do (x − b/2)² for what's inside the bracket → 3(x − 2)²
  3. 3Add last term beside the bracket → 3(x−2)² + 7
  4. 4Square the 2nd term in bracket, multiply by the number outside, then subtract → 3(x−2)² + 7 − 3×(2²)
  5. 5Simplify → 3(x − 2)² − 5

Rules of Surds
#RuleExample

2a√b − c√b = (a−c)√b7√3 − 4√3 = 3√3

Rationalizing the Denominator — 2 Cases
Case 1: Simple surd in denominator

Multiply top and bottom by the surd in the denominator.

Example: 2√8
2√8 × √8√8 = 2√88 = √22
Case 2 (Important): Surd in binomial denominator

Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate.

Conjugate of (2 + 3√5) is (2 − 3√5)

Example: 22 + 3√5
= 2(2 − 3√5)(2 + 3√5)(2 − 3√5)
= 4 − 6√54 − 45
= 4 − 6√5−41
💡 Multiplying two conjugates: just do (1st × 1st) − (2nd × 2nd). So (2+3√5)(2−3√5) = 4 − 45 = −41
Important Notes
  1. 1 If I am multiplying 2 conjugate numbers I can do: (multiply 1st term by 1st term) − (multiply 2nd by 2nd)
    (2+3√5)(2−3√5) = 4 − 45 = −41
  2. 2 √27 → if I want to convert it to a√3, find what value multiplied by 3 gives 27
    √27 = √9×3 → take the 9 outside = 3√3 ✓
  3. 3 3√4 → if I want it in form √a, then square what is outside and multiply by what is inside
    3√4 = √3²×4 = √36 ✓

H — HCF and LCM

LCM

Take everything, and if something is common take the highest power.

HCF

Take only the common parts from both, but with the lowest power.

Example: A = 2³×3²×5×7, B = 2⁵×3×7²
HCF = 2³ × 3 × 7
LCM = 2⁵ × 3² × 5 × 7²
Example: HCF and LCM of (36, 120)
36 = 2² × 3² | 120 = 2³ × 3 × 5
HCF = 2² × 3 = 12
LCM = 2³ × 3² × 5 = 360
I — Simultaneous Equations
Type 1: 2 Linear Equations — 2 methods

Method 1: Elimination

Multiply one or both equations by a number to equate coefficients, then subtract.

3x + 4y = 16 ×2 → 6x + 8y = 20 ⎫
2x + 3y = 7 ×3 → 6x + 9y = 21 ⎭
subtract ↑ → −y = −1 → y = 1
sub y=1 back in → 6x + 8(1) = 20 → 6x = 12 → x = 2

Method 2: Substitution

Make x or y the subject in one equation, then substitute into the other.

① 3x + 4y = 10 → make x subject → x = −4y + 103
②
2x + 3y = 7
2 × −4y+103 + 3y = 7
→ −8y+203 + 3y = 7 → −8y + 20 + 9y = 21 → y = 1
sub y=1 in ① → x = −4(1)+103 = 63 → x = 2
Type 2: 1 Linear + 1 Non-Linear

✦ Make x or y the subject in the linear equation, then substitute into the other (ends with Mode 5-3).

① Linear 2x + y = 1 → make y subject → y = −2x + 1
② Non-linear
x² + y² = 13
x² + (−2x+1)² = 13
x² + 4x² − 4x + 1 = 13
5x² − 4x − 12 = 0  (Mode 5-3)
x = 2
sub in ①: y = −2(2)+1
y = −3
x = −65
sub in ①: y = −2(−65)+1
y = 175
Solutions:  (2 , −3)    and    (−65 , 175)
J — Inequalities

✦ Solved exactly like an equation. There are 3 types.

⚠️ Critical Rule

If you multiply or divide by a negative number, you must FLIP the inequality sign! (> becomes <)

Linear Inequality
4x + 5 > 10
4x > 5
x > 54
Compound Inequality
3 ≤ 3x − 5 ≤ 22
8 ≤ 3x ≤ 27
83 ≤ x ≤ 9
● = included (≤ or ≥)  |  ○ = not included (< or >)
Quadratic Inequality

✦ Never solve until RHS = 0. Then use Mode 5-3 to find roots.

LHS > 0  or  LHS ≥ 0
Answer shape:
x > bigger root
x < smaller root
x² + 5x > 6
move 6 → x² + 5x − 6 > 0
(x−1)(x+6) > 0
x > 1    or    x < −6
LHS < 0  or  LHS ≤ 0
Answer shape:
smaller root < x < bigger root
x is in between the two roots
−x² + 7x − 6 < 0
already RHS=0 → −x² + 7x − 6 < 0
(x−6)(x−1) < 0
1 < x < 6
K — Subject of Formula

✦ Put the variable you want to be the subject on one side.

Example: Make Z the subject of N = 4Zm+Z
N(m + Z) = 4Z
Nm + NZ = 4Z
4Z − NZ = Nm
Z(4 − N) = Nm
Z = Nm4 − N

Circle Theorems

Key Vocabulary
Circumference= boundary / perimeter of the circle
Radius (r)= distance from centre to circumference
Diameter (d)= straight line through centre = 2r
Chord= a straight line joining two points on the circumference
Tangent= a line that touches the circle at exactly one point
Arc= a part of the circumference
The 7 Circle Theorems

Polygons

Polygon Names
4 sides = Quadrilateral 5 sides = Pentagon 6 sides = Hexagon 7 sides = Heptagon 8 sides = Octagon 9 sides = Nonagon 10 sides = Decagon
Regular vs Irregular Polygons

Regular Polygon

All sides equal, all interior angles equal, all exterior angles equal.

Sum of interior = (n−2)×180
Each interior = (n−2)×180n
Each exterior = 180 − interior = 360n
Number of sides = 360each exterior angle

Irregular Polygon

Sides and interior angles are not equal.

Sum of interior = (n−2)×180

Note: sum of exterior angles of ANY polygon always = 360°

Example — regular hexagon (n=6)
Sum interior = (6−2)×180 = 720°
Each interior = 720 ÷ 6 = 120°
Each exterior = 360 ÷ 6 = 60°

3D Shapes

Prism — Definition & Rules

✦ A prism is a shape whose cross-sectional area is constant along its entire length. The cross-section is the same shape all the way through — it never changes.

Volume= Area of Cross Section × length
C/S/A= Perimeter of Cross Section × length
T/S/A= C/S/A + 2 × Area of Cross Section
📝 The cross section is sometimes called the base of the prism.
Prism — Worked Example
ABCDEF is the cross section. ABCF = square (12 cm). FCDE = trapezium. ED = 22 cm. Height = 20 cm. Length = 80 cm. Find the total volume.
① Find the area of the cross section (ABCDEF)
The cross section = square ABCF + trapezium FCDE
Square ABCF:
Side = 12 cm   →   Area = 12 × 12 = 144 cm²
Trapezium FCDE:
Parallel sides: FC = 12 cm and ED = 22 cm
Height of trapezium = total height − square height = 20 − 12 = 8 cm
Area = (12 + 22)2 × 8 = 342 × 8 = 17 × 8 = 136 cm²
② Total area of cross section
Total cross section = 144 + 136 = 280 cm²
③ Calculate the volume
Volume = Area of cross section × length
Volume = 280 × 80 = 22 400 cm³

Similarity

What Makes Two Shapes Similar?

✦ Two shapes are similar if they have the same interior angles.

✦ If two shapes are similar, the ratio of corresponding sides is preserved.

Type 1 — Nested Triangles (Same Tip)

When a line is drawn parallel to the base, it creates two similar triangles sharing the same apex (top point).

ABAD = BCDE = ACAE
Finding a missing side
If AB=4, AD=10, BC=6 → find DE
410 = 6DE → DE = 15
Type 2 — Crossing Triangles (Bowtie / X shape)

Two triangles that cross at a point C in between — sides are proportional through the cross-point.

ABDE = ACCE = BCCD
Area & Volume Similarity
💡
Key Strategy — Always find the linear ratio k first.
Given two volumes → divide them to get the volume ratio, then take the cube root (³√) to get k.
Given two areas → divide them to get the area ratio, then take the square root (√) to get k.
Once you have k, use k² for any area and k³ for any volume.
Length ratiok = Big sideSmall side
Area ratio= k²
Volume ratio= k³
Example — two vases, volumes 405 cm³ and 960 cm³. Surface area of B = 928 cm². Find surface area of A.
Volume ratio = 960405 = k³ → k = ³√960/405 ≈ 1.333
Area ratio = k² = 1.333² ≈ 1.778
SA of A = 9281.778 = 522 cm²
f(x)

Functions

What is a Function?

✦ A function is like a black box — you put in an input x, it does operations on it, and gives you output y.

✦ Input = independent variable (x)    Output = dependent variable (y)

Evaluatef(2) → replace every x with 2 and calculate
Solvef(x) = 10 → set the function equal to 10 and solve for x
Example — f(x) = 2x + 5
f(2) = 2(2) + 5 = 9
f(x) = 10 → 2x + 5 = 10 → 2x = 5 → x = 2.5
Inverse Function f⁻¹

✦ The inverse function reverses the function — it takes the output and gives back the input.

  1. 1Replace f(x) with y
  2. 2Make x the subject
  3. 3Replace x with f⁻¹ and y with x
Example 1 — f(x) = 2x + 5
y = 2x + 5 → x = y − 52
f⁻¹(x) = x − 52
Example 2 — f(x) = 2x − 5x + 2
  1. 1Write as: y = 2x − 5x + 2
  2. 2Multiply both sides by (x + 2):   y(x + 2) = 2x − 5
  3. 3Expand:   yx + 2y = 2x − 5
  4. 4Collect all x terms on one side:   yx − 2x = −5 − 2y
  5. 5Factorise x out (HCF):   x(y − 2) = −5 − 2y
  6. 6Divide both sides by (y − 2):   x = −5 − 2yy − 2
  7. 7Replace y with x to write the inverse:   f⁻¹(x) = −5 − 2xx − 2
⚠️ Quadratic Inverse — Complete the Square First

If f(x) is quadratic (has an x² term), you cannot rearrange directly. First rewrite using completing the square, then make x the subject.

Example — find f⁻¹(x) where f(x) = x² + 6x + 5
  1. 1
    Complete the square:   x² + 6x + 5 = (x + 3)² − 9 + 5 = (x + 3)² − 4
  2. 2
    Write as y = (x + 3)² − 4, then rearrange to make x the subject:
  3. 3
    y + 4 = (x + 3)²   →   √y + 4 = x + 3
  4. 4
    x = √y + 4 − 3   →   replace y with x:   f⁻¹(x) = √x + 4 − 3
Composite Functions fg(x)

✦ fg(x) means: first apply g, then apply f to the result. Think of it as f inside g.

Example — f(x) = 2x + 5    g(x) = 3x − 8
Finding fg(x) — apply g first, then f
Step 1 — substitute g into f:   fg(x) = f(3x − 8)
Step 2 — replace x in f(x) = 2x + 5 with (3x − 8):   2(3x − 8) + 5
Step 3 — expand and simplify:   6x − 16 + 5 = 6x − 11
Finding gf(x) — apply f first, then g
Step 1 — substitute f into g:   gf(x) = g(2x + 5)
Step 2 — replace x in g(x) = 3x − 8 with (2x + 5):   3(2x + 5) − 8
Step 3 — expand and simplify:   6x + 15 − 8 = 6x + 7
Substituting a number — find fg(3) using f(x) = 2x + 5, g(x) = 3x − 8
fg(3) — apply g first, then f
Step 1 — apply g to 3 first:   g(3) = 3(3) − 8 = 9 − 8 = 1
Step 2 — now apply f to that result:   f(1) = 2(1) + 5 = 7
gf(3) — apply f first, then g
Step 1 — apply f to 3 first:   f(3) = 2(3) + 5 = 6 + 5 = 11
Step 2 — now apply g to that result:   g(11) = 3(11) − 8 = 33 − 8 = 25
💡 fg(x) ≠ gf(x) in general. The order matters! Think of it as: whichever letter is written second (nearest to the x) is applied first.

Graph Transformations

Graph Transformations of f(x)
📦 OUTSIDE the bracket
Affects the Y coordinate
Do exactly what it says:
+ a → Y goes up by a
× a → Y gets multiplied by a
🔀 INSIDE the bracket
Affects the X coordinate
Do the opposite:
+ a → X goes left (subtract a)
× a → X gets divided by a
TransformationEffect on Graph
y = f(x) + aShift up by a (if a positive) or down (if a negative)
y = f(x + a)Shift left by a (if a positive) or right (if a negative)
y = af(x)Stretch vertically by scale factor a
y = f(ax)Stretch horizontally by scale factor 1a
Turning point at (−6, −4). Find turning point of y = f(x) + 5
+5 is OUTSIDE → affects Y → Y + 5 → (−6, +1)
Turning point at (−6, −4). Find turning point of y = f(3x)
3 is INSIDE → affects X → X ÷ 3 → (−2, −4)

Calculus

Differentiation Rules

✦ Differentiation gives you y' (also written dydx) — this tells you the gradient (slope) of the curve at any point. Think of it as: how steep is the curve right here?

✦ Before you differentiate, make sure every term is added or subtracted — no brackets, no x stuck in the bottom of a fraction. Always clean up the expression first.

y = axⁿ→ y' = anxⁿ⁻¹   (multiply by the power, then reduce the power by 1)
y = ax→ y' = a   (just the number in front)
y = a (constant)→ y' = 0   (a flat number has no slope)
Example 1 — y = 3x² + x + 8
y' = 6x + 1
Example 2 — y = 3x² + 1x   → rewrite 1x as x⁻¹ first
y = 3x² + x⁻¹ → y' = 6x − x⁻² = 6x − 1x²
Example 3 — y = 8√x + 3x⁵   → rewrite √x as x½ first
y = 8x½ + 3x⁵ → y' = 4x−½ + 15x⁴ = 4√x + 15x⁴
Example 4 — y = (x + 5)²   → expand the bracket first
y = x² + 10x + 25 → y' = 2x + 10
⚠️ When x is in the denominator

If you have a fraction with x on the bottom — expand the top first, then split into separate terms by dividing each one by x. This gets x back to the top so you can differentiate normally.

y = (x + 5)²x = x² + 10x + 25x = x + 10 + 25x = x + 10 + 25x⁻¹ → y' = 1 − 25x²
🔑 Stationary / Turning Points (max & min)
⚠️ Key words to watch for: maximum, minimum, stationary point, turning point. These all mean the same thing — differentiate and set equal to zero.
At a stationary point the curve is flat — the gradient = 0. So:
Step 1: Differentiate y → get y'
Step 2: Set y' = 0 and solve for x
Step 3: Substitute x back into the original equation to get y
Find the stationary point of y = x³ − 3x² − 9x + 5
Step 1 — Differentiate:   y' = 3x² − 6x − 9
Step 2 — Set y' = 0:   3x² − 6x − 9 = 0   →   x² − 2x − 3 = 0   →   (x−3)(x+1) = 0
x = 3   or   x = −1
Step 3 — Find y values:
x = 3:   y = 27 − 27 − 27 + 5 = −22   → minimum point (3, −22)
x = −1:   y = −1 − 3 + 9 + 5 = 10   → maximum point (−1, 10)
📐 Maximum Area / Volume Problems

✦ These questions give you a shape and ask for the maximum area or volume. The trick is: you need to get the expression down to one variable only, then treat it like a normal stationary point.

  1. 1
    Read the question. You will usually get two pieces of information — for example, the area formula and the perimeter. Use one to substitute into the other so everything is in terms of one letter (e.g. just x).
  2. 2
    Now you have one expression — differentiate it.
  3. 3
    Set the derivative = 0 and solve for x — this gives the value at which the area/volume is maximum.
  4. 4
    Substitute x back into the area/volume formula to find the maximum value.
Photo frame: width = x cm, height = y cm, perimeter = 72 cm. (a) Show A = 36x − x²   (b) Find dA/dx   (c) Find max A
Part (a) — Show A = 36x − x²
Perimeter = 72 → 2x + 2y = 72 → y = 36 − x
Area A = x × y = x(36 − x) = 36x − x² ✓
Part (b) — Find dAdx
A = 36x − x²   →   dAdx = 36 − 2x
Part (c) — Find maximum value of A
Set dAdx = 0:   36 − 2x = 0   →   x = 18
Max A = 36(18) − 18² = 648 − 324 = 324 cm²
💡 How to Read the Question — What to Do
💡 The question won't always say "differentiate." You have to recognise what it's asking from the words it uses. Here's how to decode it:
📍 He gives you coordinates
If the question gives you a point like (2, 5) or says "the curve passes through (3, 7)" — substitute the x value into the original equation to check or find the y value. You don't differentiate here.
Example: y = x² + 3. Point is at x = 2 → y = 4 + 3 = 7
📐 He mentions gradient
If the question says anything about a gradient — "find the point where the gradient is 4", "the tangent has gradient 6" — then:
1. Differentiate to get y'
2. Set y' = the gradient value he gave you and solve for x
3. Substitute that x into the original equation to get y
Example: y = x² + 2x, gradient = 6 → y' = 2x + 2 = 6 → x = 2 → y = 4 + 4 = 8 → point is (2, 8)
📈 He asks for tangent or normal at a point
Tangent: differentiate → substitute x to get gradient m → use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
Normal: exact same steps but the gradient of the normal = −1m (flip and negate)
🔝 He says max / min / stationary / turning point
Differentiate → set y' = 0 → solve for x → substitute back into original equation to get y.
Kinematics — Motion Calculus

✦ When an object moves, its position, speed, and acceleration are all linked. Differentiate once to go from position to speed. Differentiate again to go from speed to acceleration.

Displacement (s)
→ differentiate →
Velocity (v)
→ differentiate →
Acceleration (a)
Example — s = 4t² − 9t, find velocity at t = 5
Rewrite: s = 4t² − 9t⁻¹
v = dsdt = 8t + 9t⁻² = 8t + 9t²
At t = 5: v = 8(5) + 925 = 40 + 0.36 = 40.36 m/s

Proportionality

Direct vs Inverse Proportionality

Direct Proportional (y ∝ x)

If one increases, the other increases and vice versa.

y = kx
k = constant of proportionality

Inversely Proportional (y ∝ 1x)

If one increases, the other decreases and vice versa.

y = kx
k = constant of proportionality
How to Solve Proportionality Problems
  1. 1Write the proportionality statement (y = kxⁿ or y = kxⁿ)
  2. 2Substitute the given values to find k
  3. 3Write the full equation with k, then answer the question
Example — T is directly proportional to √x. T = 400 when x = 625.
T = k√x
400 = k√625 = 25k → k = 16
Full equation: T = 16√x
When x = 56.25: T = 16√56.25 = 16×7.5 = 120
📝 Common types: y ∝ x², y ∝ x³, y ∝ √x, y ∝ 1x², y ∝ 1√x. Always read carefully what the proportionality is.
Graph or Table Questions — How to Handle Them

✦ Some questions give you a graph or a table of values instead of telling you the relationship directly. You need to figure it out yourself.

📈 Direct Proportion (y ∝ xⁿ)
As x goes up, y goes up.
The graph curves upward from the origin.
Write y = kxⁿ
📉 Inverse Proportion (y ∝ 1/xⁿ)
As x goes up, y goes down.
The graph curves down steeply from the y-axis.
Write y = kxⁿ
💡 Once you know if it's direct or inverse — pick any one pair of values from the graph or table, substitute them into y = kxⁿ (or y = k/xⁿ) and solve for k. Then write the full equation.
Example 1 — Graph question (direct)
R ∝ t². The graph shows R at t = 4 is 40. Find the formula for R.
Write: R = kt²
At t = 4, R = 40:   40 = k × 16   →   k = 4016 = 2.5
R = 2.5t²
Example 2 — Table question (inverse)
(a) Find a formula for y in terms of x.   (b) Find x when y = 144.
Part (a)
y is inversely proportional to x² → write: y = kx²
Pick any pair from the table — use x = 2, y = 9:
9 = k4   →   k = 36
y = 36x²
Part (b)
144 = 36x²   →   x² = 36144 = 0.25   →   x = 0.5
…

Sequences

Arithmetic Sequence Formulas
📋 STEP 1 — Before anything
Always write down a and d at the start of every question. If you don't have them, your first job is to find them.
🔀 Which formula to use?
Question says "sum" → use Sₙ
No mention of sum → use Uₙ (nth term)
Uₙ= a + d(n − 1)    ← use when NOT asked for a sum
Sₙ= n2 × [2a + d(n − 1)]    ← use when asked for a SUM
Sₙ= n2 × [a + L]    ← only use this when the last term L is given (rare)
VariableMeaning
nterm number (n > 0)
afirst term
dcommon difference (Uₙ₊₁ − Uₙ)
Uₙnth term
Sₙsum of first n terms
Llast term
💡 Many questions don't give you a and d directly — they give you two pieces of information (e.g. U₃ = 11 and U₇ = 27). Set up two equations and solve simultaneously to find a and d first, then answer the question.
Worked Examples
Find nth term — sequence: 6, 10, 14, 18, ...
a = 6, d = 4 (difference between terms)
Uₙ = 6 + 4(n−1) = 6 + 4n − 4 = 4n + 2
Sum of first 10 terms — a = 3, d = 5
S₁₀ = 102[2(3) + 5(10−1)] = 5[6 + 45] = 255
💡 The (n+1)th term of the sequence above is just Uₙ with n replaced by (n+1): U(n+1) = 4(n+1) + 2 = 4n + 6
Question Type 1 — Find a and d Using Simultaneous Equations

✦ When a question gives you two pieces of information (e.g. the 2nd term and the 5th term), you can write two equations using Uₙ = a + d(n−1) and solve simultaneously to find a and d.

  1. 1
    Write Uₙ for each piece of information given → you get two equations in a and d.
  2. 2
    Subtract one equation from the other to eliminate a → find d.
  3. 3
    Substitute d back into either equation to find a.
  4. 4
    Now you have a and d — use whichever formula the question needs (Uₙ or Sₙ).
S = 292, U₂ = 8.5, U₅ = 13. Find N.
① Use Uₙ = a + (n−1)d — write two equations
U₂:   a + (2−1)d = 8.5  →  a + d = 8.5   ... (1)
U₅:   a + (5−1)d = 13  →  a + 4d = 13   ... (2)
② Subtract (1) from (2)
(a + 4d) − (a + d) = 13 − 8.5  →  3d = 4.5  →  d = 1.5
③ Substitute d = 1.5 into (1) to find a
a + 1.5 = 8.5  →  a = 7
④ Use Sₙ = n2[2a + (n−1)d] = 292, substitute a = 7, d = 1.5
N2[2(7) + (N−1)(1.5)] = 292
N2[14 + 1.5N − 1.5] = 292  →  N2[12.5 + 1.5N] = 292
N(12.5 + 1.5N) = 584  →  1.5N² + 12.5N − 584 = 0  (×2) →  3N² + 25N − 1168 = 0
⑤ Quadratic formula
N = −25 ± √625 + 140166 = −25 ± 1216  →  N = 966 = 16
Question Type 2 — Find d When Terms are Given as Expressions

✦ Sometimes the terms are written as algebraic expressions (like k, 3k/4, k/2...). Find d by subtracting consecutive terms, then use the given information to set up an equation and solve for k.

Terms: k, 3k/4, k/2, k/4. U₁₅ = 90 + 2k. Find S₃₀.
① Find a and d from the terms
a = k  (first term)    d = 3k4 − k = 3k − 4k4 = −k4
② Use Uₙ = a + (n−1)d, write U₁₅ and substitute a and d
U₁₅ = a + (15−1)d = k + 14 × (−k4) = k − 14k4 = −2.5k
③ Set equal to the given U₁₅ = 90 + 2k and solve for k
−2.5k = 90 + 2k  →  −4.5k = 90  →  k = −20
④ Find actual values: a = −20, d = 5
a = k = −20    d = −k4 = −(−20)4 = 5
⑤ Use Sₙ = n2[2a + (n−1)d], substitute a = −20, d = 5, n = 30
S₃₀ = 302[2(−20) + (30−1)(5)] = 15 × [−40 + 29 × 5] = 15 × [−40 + 145] = 15 × 105 = 1575
Question Type 3 — Sum Between Two Terms (e.g. 50th to 100th)

✦ If the question asks for the sum from the 50th term to the 100th term, you cannot just do S₁₀₀ alone. You need to subtract the terms you don't want.

Sum from 50th to 100th = S₁₀₀ − S₄₉
Why S₄₉ and not S₅₀? Because you want to keep the 50th term — so you subtract everything before it, which is the first 49 terms. If you subtracted S₅₀ you would remove the 50th term too, which you need.
Sequence: 8, 15, 22, 29, 36, ...   Find the sum from the 50th to the 100th term inclusive.
① Write a and d
a = 8    d = 15 − 8 = 7
② Use Sₙ = n2[2a + (n−1)d] — calculate S₁₀₀, substitute a = 8, d = 7, n = 100
S₁₀₀ = 1002[2(8) + (100−1)(7)] = 50 × [16 + 99 × 7] = 50 × [16 + 693] = 50 × 709 = 35 450
③ Calculate S₄₉ — substitute a = 8, d = 7, n = 49
S₄₉ = 492[2(8) + (49−1)(7)] = 24.5 × [16 + 48 × 7] = 24.5 × [16 + 336] = 24.5 × 352 = 8 624
④ Subtract
S₁₀₀ − S₄₉ = 35 450 − 8 624 = 26 826
⚠️ Always ask yourself: which term is the first one I want to keep? Subtract all terms before that one. If you want to keep term 50, subtract S₄₉.
→

Vectors

What is a Vector?

✦ A vector has both magnitude (size) and direction.

✦ Written as a column vector with brackets:  (xy)  — x is horizontal movement, y is vertical movement.

⚠️ DIRECTION IS EVERYTHING
The arrow on top of a vector tells you which way you're travelling.
If you move in the opposite direction to a known vector — multiply it by −1.
Example: if →OA = 2a, then →AO = −2a  (same line, opposite direction)
Magnitude|v| = √x² + y²
Position vectora vector from the origin O to a point
Vector Operations

Add / Subtract

(32) + (1−4) = (4−2)

Add x's together, add y's together

Multiply by scalar

3 × (25) = (615)

Multiply each component by the scalar

Finding AB using position vectors

✦ To go from A to B: travel backwards from A → O (flip sign), then forwards O → B.

→AB = −→OA + →OB = →OB − →OA
Parallel Vectors & Collinear Points

Parallel Vectors

Two vectors are parallel if one = K × the other (K is a constant).

K positive → same direction  |  K negative → opposite direction

Collinear Points (same line)

A, B, C are collinear if →AB = K × →BC for some constant K.

How to Find an Unknown Point (e.g. intersection P)
⚠️ Used when point P lies on two different lines and you need its vector. Build 2 equations, then compare coefficients to solve.
  1. 1
    Find every vector you can from the diagram. Walk along each line from point to point. Get all vectors before introducing any unknown constants.
  2. 2
    Every time you identify a new line, find its vector immediately. Don't leave any line without a vector expression.
  3. 3
    Equation 1 (easy path) — P lies on line OC, so OP is a fraction of OC. Write: OP = k × OC where k is unknown. Label this Eq.1.
  4. 4
    Equation 2 (second path) — reach P a different way: OP = OA + AP. Since P is on line AB, write AP = t × AB. So: OP = OA + t × AB. Expand, collect a and b terms. Label this Eq.2.
  5. 5
    Compare coefficients — Eq.1 = Eq.2 = OP. Set the coefficient of a in Eq.1 equal to the coefficient of a in Eq.2, and same for b. This gives two simple equations.
  6. 6
    Solve for k (or t), then substitute back into Eq.1 to get the final vector for OP.
Example — OACB trapezium. OA = 2a, OB = 5b, AC = 3b. Find OP where P is the intersection of OC and AB.
① Find all vectors first
→OC = →OA + →AC = 2a + 3b
→AB = →AO + →OB = −2a + 5b    (AO = −OA, flip the sign)
② Equation 1 — P lies on OC
→OP = k(2a + 3b) = 2ka + 3kb    Eq.1
③ Equation 2 — reach P via O → A → P
→OP = →OA + t · →AB = 2a + t(−2a + 5b)
= (2 − 2t)a + 5tb    Eq.2
④ Compare coefficients
Coeff. of a:   2k = 2 − 2t   →   k = 1 − t
Coeff. of b:   3k = 5t       →   k = 5t3
⑤ Solve
1 − t = 5t3   →   3 − 3t = 5t   →   8t = 3   →   t = 38
k = 1 − 38 = 58
Substitute into Eq.1:   →OP = 58(2a + 3b) = 54a + 158b
🔄

Transformations

What You Must State for Each Type
TypeWhat You Need to Describe It
TranslationThe translation vector (xy)
RotationAngle, centre of rotation, and direction (clockwise / anticlockwise)
EnlargementCentre of enlargement and scale factor
ReflectionEquation of the mirror line
🔁 Rotation — How to Do It
  1. 1
    Get a piece of tracing paper. Place it on top of the original shape and trace the shape onto it. Also draw a small upward-pointing arrow ↑ on the tracing paper — this is your reference direction.
  2. 2
    Put your finger (or pencil tip) firmly on the centre of rotation (e.g. (0, 0)) so the paper pivots around that exact point.
  3. 3
    Rotate the tracing paper in the direction stated:
    Clockwise 90°
    ↑ arrow rotates to point → (right)
    Anticlockwise 90°
    ↑ arrow rotates to point ← (left)
    180°
    ↑ arrow rotates to point ↓ (down)
    270° clockwise
    ↑ arrow rotates to point ← (left)
  4. 4
    Mark the new position of the shape on the grid. That is your rotated image.
➡️ Translation — How to Do It

✦ A translation moves every point of the shape by the same amount. The shape does not rotate or resize.

Given vector (34):   move every point +3 on x (right) and +4 on y (up).
Negative values: −3 on x means move left 3.   −4 on y means move down 4.
Point A is at (1, 2). Translate by (3−2)
New position = (1 + 3, 2 − 2) = (4, 0)
🪞 Reflection — How to Do It
  1. 1
    Draw the mirror line clearly on the grid (e.g. y = x, x = 2, y = −1).
  2. 2
    For each vertex of the shape, count how many steps it takes to reach the mirror line perpendicularly (at a right angle).
  3. 3
    Continue the same number of steps on the other side of the mirror line. Think of the line as a mirror — the image is the same distance behind it.
  4. 4
    Connect the new points to draw the reflected shape.
Common Mirror Lines
Mirror LineWhat happens to coordinates
x-axis  (y = 0)(x, y) → (x, −y)   — flip the y
y-axis  (x = 0)(x, y) → (−x, y)   — flip the x
y = x(x, y) → (y, x)   — swap x and y
y = −x(x, y) → (−y, −x)   — swap and negate both
🔍 Enlargement — How to Do It
  1. 1
    Mark the centre of enlargement on the grid.
  2. 2
    For each vertex of the shape, count the number of steps from the centre to that vertex — horizontally and vertically.
  3. 3
    Multiply those steps by the scale factor. Move that many steps from the centre in the same direction to find the new vertex position.
  4. 4
    Connect all the new vertices to draw the enlarged shape.
Centre (1, 1), scale factor 2. Vertex A is at (3, 2).
Steps from centre to A:   right 2, up 1
Multiply by scale factor 2:   right 4, up 2
New vertex A' = (1 + 4, 1 + 2) = (5, 3)
💡 Negative scale factor — do the same steps but move in the opposite direction from the centre. The image ends up on the other side, upside down.
🎯 Finding the Centre of Enlargement (when both shapes are given)

✦ If the question gives you both shapes (original and enlarged) and asks you to find the centre of enlargement — you don't need to count steps. Just draw lines.

  1. 1
    Pick a corner (vertex) on the original shape. Find the matching corner on the enlarged shape — the one that corresponds to it (e.g. both are the top-left corner).
  2. 2
    Draw a straight line passing through both of those matching corners. Extend the line in both directions.
  3. 3
    Repeat for another pair of matching corners — draw a second line through them and extend it.
  4. 4
    The point where all the lines cross is the centre of enlargement.
⚠️ You only need two lines to find the crossing point, but drawing a third is a good check. If all three meet at the same point — you know you've got it right.

Statistics

Key Measures — Formulas
Mean= Sum of all valuesNumber of values   — add everything up, divide by how many there are
Mode= The value that appears the most often
Range= Largest value − Smallest value
Median= N + 12th value   — sort first, then find the middle position
Lower Q (LQ)= N + 14th value   — middle of the lower half
Upper Q (UQ)= 3(N + 1)4th value   — middle of the upper half
IQR= UQ − LQ   — spread of the middle 50% of data
💡 If the position formula gives a decimal (e.g. 3.5th value), take the average of the 3rd and 4th values. If it gives 2.25th, take the 2nd value and add 0.25 of the gap to the 3rd.
Worked Example — N = 11
Dataset (unsorted):   10, 5, 6, 12, 12, 23, 28, 14, 9, 3, 17    (N = 11)
① Sort the data first — always
3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 12, 12, 14, 17, 23, 28
①3 ②5 ③6 ← LQ ④9 ⑤10 ⑥12 ← median ⑦12 ⑧14 ⑨17 ← UQ ⑩23 ⑪28
② Calculate each measure
Mean = 3 + 5 + 6 + 9 + 10 + 12 + 12 + 14 + 17 + 23 + 2811 = 13911 = 12.6
Mode = 12   (appears twice, all others once)
Range = 28 − 3 = 25
Median position = 11 + 12 = 6th value = 12
LQ position = 11 + 14 = 3rd value = 6
UQ position = 3(12)4 = 9th value = 17
IQR = 17 − 6 = 11
Grouped Data — Mean from Frequency Table

✦ You don't have the exact values — only class intervals. Use the midpoint of each class as an estimate for the values in it.

  1. 1Find the midpoint of each class: midpoint = lower + upper2
  2. 2Multiply midpoint × frequency for each row → this is fx
  3. 3Mean = Σ(fx)Σf   (sum of all fx ÷ total frequency)
The table shows the ages of 40 people at a gym.
Age (years)Frequency (f)Midpoint (x)fx
10 ≤ age < 2061590
20 ≤ age < 301125275
30 ≤ age < 401435490
40 ≤ age < 50745315
50 ≤ age < 60255110
Total40—1280
Mean = 128040 = 32 years
Combined Mean — Two Groups

✦ If a question gives you the mean of one group and the mean of another group, and asks for the overall mean — you cannot just average the two means. You need the total sum of each group first.

Formula:   Total sum = mean × number of people   →   Overall mean = Total sum of all groupsTotal number of people
On Monday, 8 students sat a test. Their mean score was 14. On Wednesday, 5 different students sat the same test. Their mean score was 11. Find the mean score of all 13 students.
Step 1 — Find Monday's total:   8 × 14 = 112
Step 2 — Find Wednesday's total:   5 × 11 = 55
Step 3 — Combined total:   112 + 55 = 167
Step 4 — Overall mean:   16713 = 12.8
⚠️ Never add the two means and divide by 2 — that only works if both groups have the same number of people. Always go back to totals first.
Cumulative Frequency Curves

✦ A cumulative frequency curve shows a running total of frequencies. It always goes up and forms an S-shape.

  1. 1Build a cumulative frequency table by adding up frequencies one by one (each row = previous total + current frequency)
  2. 2Plot cumulative frequency on the y-axis against the upper class boundary on the x-axis. Always use the bigger/upper value of each class — e.g. for the class 10–20, plot at 20.
  3. 3Join the points with a smooth S-shaped curve — never straight lines
  4. 4Read off values: draw a horizontal line from the required cumulative frequency to the curve, then drop down to the x-axis
Median
Read at N2
Lower Q
Read at N4
Upper Q
Read at 3N4

Standard Form

Standard Form Format
Forma × 10ⁿ   where   1 ≤ a < 10
⬅️ Moving decimal LEFT
Power increases (+)
e.g. 9 880 000 → move left 6 places → 9.88 × 10⁶
➡️ Moving decimal RIGHT
Power decreases (−)
e.g. 0.00045 → move right 4 places → 4.5 × 10⁻⁴
Converting to standard form
9 880 000 = 9.88 × 10⁶
0.00045 = 4.5 × 10⁻⁴
Adding / Subtracting in Standard Form

✦ Make all numbers have the same power of 10, then add/subtract the numbers in front normally.

3×10⁵ + 2×10³
Make both ×10⁵ → 3×10⁵ + 0.02×10⁵
Add the coefficients → (3 + 0.02) × 10⁵ = 3.02 × 10⁵
1.88×10⁷ + 3.10×10⁸ + 2.64×10⁸ + 7.18×10⁷
Convert all to ×10⁸ → 0.188×10⁸ + 3.10×10⁸ + 2.64×10⁸ + 0.718×10⁸
= (0.188 + 3.10 + 2.64 + 0.718) × 10⁸ = 6.646 × 10⁸

Interest

Simple vs Compound Interest
⭐ Exam tip:   Compound interest comes up far more in exams than simple interest. Focus on mastering the compound formula — simple interest is rarely tested and is straightforward when it is.
Simple Interest
I =PRT100
A =I + P
I = Interest   P = Principal amount
R = Rate (%)   T = Time in years
A = Final amount
Compound Interest
A =P(1 + R100)t
I =A − P
A = Final amount   P = Principal
R = Rate (%)   t = Time in years
Worked Examples
Kwo invests HK$40,000 for 3 years at 2.5% per year compound interest
A = 40000 × (1 + 2.5100)³ = 40000 × (1.025)³
A = 40000 × 1.0769 = HK$43,076.56
Mabintou invests $7,500 for 3 years at 4% per year compound interest
A = 7500 × (1.04)³ = 7500 × 1.1249 = $8,436.67
💡 The key difference: in simple interest, you only earn interest on the original amount. In compound interest, you earn interest on the interest too — so your money grows faster.

Trigonometric Curves

General Form: y = a cos(bx + c) + d
💡 When the question gives you a graph and asks for a, b, c, d — follow these steps in order. Always find a, d, b first, then use substitution to get c.
① Find a (amplitude)
a = ymax − ymin2
This controls how tall the wave is.
② Find d (vertical shift)
d = ymax + ymin2
This is where the midline sits.
③ Find b (frequency)
b = 360°wavelength
Wavelength = distance from peak to peak (or trough to trough).
④ Find c (phase shift)
Substitute a, b, d into the equation. Then pick any known point (x, y) from the graph and solve for c.
⚠️ Range check:   After finding c, check it falls in the required range. If not — add or subtract 360° until it does.
Worked Example — y = a cos(bx°) + c
⚠️ The question uses letters a, b, c — where c here is the vertical shift (what we call d in the general formula). Don't confuse it with a phase shift. Just use the letters the question gives you.
From the graph: ymax = 3, ymin = −1. Peaks at x = 0, 120, 240 → wavelength = 120°.
① Find a (amplitude)
a = ymax − ymin2 = 3 − (−1)2 = 42 = 2
② Find c — the vertical shift (c in this question = d in the general formula)
c = ymax + ymin2 = 3 + (−1)2 = 22 = 1
③ Find b
Wavelength = 120° (peak to peak distance)
b = 360120 = 3
④ Final answer
a = 2,   b = 3,   c = 1
Full equation: y = 2cos(3x°) + 1
Basic Graph Shapes — Reference
y = sin x
y = cos x
y = tan x
Dashed yellow lines = asymptotes (tan is undefined at 90°, 270°). Repeats every 180°.

Ratio

What is a Ratio?

✦ A ratio compares two or more quantities.   e.g. 3 : 4 means for every 3 of one thing, there are 4 of another.

✦ Ratios can be simplified just like fractions — divide both sides by the HCF.

✦ To share an amount in a ratio, find the value of one part first:   Total ÷ (sum of parts) = 1 part.

🔑 Key Strategy — Always find everything first
Before you answer anything, extract all the information you can from the ratio:
1. Use the ratio to find the actual number of people/items in each group.
2. Convert any percentages or fractions given for each group into actual numbers.
3. Add up all the full-time workers, divide by the total — that gives you the fraction or percentage.
💡 Ratio and percentage link: Once you use the ratio to find how many people are in each group, any percentage given for that group just means: multiply that group's size by the percentage. Then combine all groups to get the overall answer.
🔑 How to Set Up a Ratio Table

✦ The best way to solve ratio questions is to write the ratio in a table with the values underneath. Whatever the question gives you — write it in the correct column, then cross-multiply to find the rest.

Group AGroup BTotal
3 4 7
?  (cross-mult) ?  (cross-mult) given = 280

✦ Cross-multiplication:   Group A actual = 3 × 2807 = 120    Group B actual = 4 × 2807 = 160

✦ Write everything you know in the table first — then fill the gaps. This stops you from missing anything.

Example 1 — Three-Part Ratio (Linked Ratios)
Green : Orange = 2 : 3    Orange : Yellow = 1 : 5    Total = 280. Find number of green sweets.
① Set up both ratios as separate tables
GreenOrange
2 3
??
OrangeYellow
1 5
??
② Use Orange as the link between the two ratios
In ratio 1: Orange = 3 parts    In ratio 2: Orange = 1 part
Make Orange the same in both → multiply ratio 2 by 3:   Orange : Yellow = 3 : 15
Now write the full table:   Green : Orange : Yellow = 2 : 3 : 15  → total = 20 parts
GreenOrangeYellowTotal
2 3 15 20
? ? ? 280
③ Cross-multiply to find Green
1 part = 28020 = 14
Green = 2 × 14 = 28
Example 2 — Ratio + Fractions/Percentages Mixed
120 children. Girls : Boys = 3 : 5.   16/25 of boys go climbing.   Twice as many girls go sailing as climbing.   Find total sailing.
① Write the ratio table — total given as 120
GirlsBoysTotal
3 5 8
? ? 120
Girls = 3 × 1208 = 45     Boys = 5 × 1208 = 75
② Find boys who go climbing and sailing
Boys climbing = 1625 × 75 = 48
Boys sailing = 75 − 48 = 27
③ Find girls who go climbing and sailing
"Twice as many girls go sailing as climbing" → let girls climbing = x, then girls sailing = 2x
Total girls: x + 2x = 45 → 3x = 45 → x = 15
Girls climbing = 15    Girls sailing = 2 × 15 = 30
④ Total children sailing
Boys sailing + Girls sailing = 27 + 30 = 57

Percentage

Key Rule

✦ Always set up as: Old : increase or decrease : New — where Old is always 100

Old : change : New
→
100 : % : (100 ± %)
Always put 100 in the Old column. Cross multiply to find x.
Example
All clothes had a 30% sale. A T-shirt costs £80 in the sale. What was the original price?
Old decrease New 100 30 70 x 80

3D Trigonometry

Key Strategy — Break Into 2D Triangles

✦ In any 3D trig problem, you will always find the answer by using two separate 2D triangles — one to find an intermediate length, then another to find the angle or final length.

  1. 1Identify the angle you need (e.g. angle AHF in a cuboid)
  2. 2Identify which sides form the triangle containing that angle
  3. 3Use Pythagoras on the base triangle to find the diagonal base length
  4. 4Use that length in the vertical triangle to find the angle using tan⁻¹
Worked Example — Angle from Corner of a Cuboid
📦 Cuboid: EF = 17 cm, GF = 5 cm, AF = 8 cm. Find angle HAF where H is opposite corner on base.
  1. 1Find HF (diagonal across base)
  2. 2HF = √17² + 5² = √314
  3. 3Now use triangle AHF: AF = 8 (height), HF = √314
  4. 4tan θ = AFHF = 8√314
  5. 5θ = tan⁻¹(8√314) = 24.3°
🧭

Bearing

What is a Bearing?

✦ A bearing is an angle measured from North, going clockwise.

✦ Bearings are always written as 3 digits — e.g. 045°, 120°, 270°.

📐 Protractor Tip — Angles bigger than 180°
Bearings are always measured clockwise from North. A normal protractor only goes up to 180°, so:

If the bearing is less than 180° — measure clockwise normally. No problem.

If the bearing is more than 180° — it is easier to flip the protractor and measure the remaining angle going anticlockwise, then subtract from 360°.

Example: You want to draw a bearing of 250°.
Instead of trying to measure 250° clockwise, calculate: 360° − 250° = 110°.
Now measure 110° anticlockwise from North — you end up at exactly the same direction as 250° clockwise. ✓

How to Find a Bearing — Steps
  1. 1
    Draw a North line at the point you are measuring FROM (the question says "bearing of X from Y" — draw North at Y).
  2. 2
    Draw a line from that point toward the target.
  3. 3
    Measure the angle clockwise from North to that line.
  4. 4
    If the problem needs calculation (not just reading), use alternate angles (North lines are parallel → Z-angles / co-interior angles apply) and triangle angle rules to find the answer.
  5. 5
    Write the answer as 3 digits. If you get 47°, write 047°.
💡 Key angle rules used in bearing questions: All North lines are parallel to each other — so you can use alternate angles (Z-angles = equal) and co-interior angles (add to 180°) between them.
🔑 Exam Hint — What Most Bearing Questions Need
Most bearing calculation questions involve a triangle between two or three points. To solve them you will almost always need:

1. The U-shape rule (co-interior angles) — when two North lines are on the same side and face each other, the two angles between them add up to 180°. This is the most common tool for finding the angle inside the triangle.

2. Sine rule or Cosine rule — once you have the angle inside the triangle, use these to find missing sides or angles, exactly as you did in 1H.

The usual order: draw the diagram → draw both North lines → use the U-shape to find the triangle angle → apply sine/cosine rule → convert back to a bearing.
Worked Example
Given: AB = 150m, AC = 275m, bearing of C from A = 120°. B is due north of A. Find bearing of C from B.
① Find angle BAC
B is due North of A → North line at A points to B. Bearing of C from A = 120° clockwise from North.
So angle BAC = 120° (measured from AB to AC, clockwise)
② Use cosine rule to find BC
BC² = AB² + AC² − 2 × AB × AC × cos(BAC)
BC² = 150² + 275² − 2(150)(275)cos(120°)
BC² = 22500 + 75625 − 82500 × (−0.5)
BC² = 22500 + 75625 + 41250 = 139375
BC = 373.3 m
③ Find angle ABC using sine rule
sin(ABC)275 = sin(120°)373.3
sin(ABC) = 275 × sin(120°)373.3 ≈ 0.638
Angle ABC = sin⁻¹(0.638) ≈ 39.6°
④ Find the bearing of C from B
North lines at A and B are parallel → co-interior angles add to 180°.
Angle between North at B and line BC = 180° − 39.6° = 140.4°
Bearing of C from B = 140°

Construction

Type 1 — Perpendicular Bisector of a Line

✦ The perpendicular bisector cuts a line exactly in half at 90°. Any point on this bisector is equidistant from both endpoints.

  1. 1
    Open your compass to more than half the length of the line.
  2. 2
    Place the compass point on one end of the line (e.g. D). Draw an arc above and below the line.
  3. 3
    Without changing the compass width, place it on the other end (E). Draw arcs above and below — they should cross the first arcs.
  4. 4
    Use a ruler to draw a straight line through the two intersection points of the arcs. This is the perpendicular bisector.
⚠️ Leave all construction arcs visible — never rub them out. The examiner needs to see them.
Type 2 — Angle Bisector

✦ The angle bisector cuts an angle exactly in half. Any point on this bisector is equidistant from both arms of the angle.

  1. 1
    Place compass point at the vertex B. Draw an arc that crosses both arms of the angle (BA and BC).
  2. 2
    Place compass point at the point where the arc crosses arm BA. Draw a small arc inside the angle.
  3. 3
    Without changing the compass width, place it where the arc crosses arm BC. Draw another small arc — it should cross the previous one.
  4. 4
    Draw a straight line from B through the intersection point of the two small arcs. This is the angle bisector.
⚠️ Leave all construction arcs visible — never rub them out. The examiner needs to see them.
✍️

Proofs

How to Represent Numbers in Proofs
⚠️ Always read the question very carefully. It will tell you exactly what kind of numbers you are dealing with — consecutive, even, odd, etc. Use the correct representation below.
3 Consecutive Numbers
n
n + 1
n + 2
3 Consecutive Even Numbers
2n
2n + 2
2n + 4
3 Consecutive Odd Numbers
2n + 1
2n + 3
2n + 5

✦ Any even number can be written as 2n (a multiple of 2).

✦ Any odd number can be written as 2n + 1 (one more than a multiple of 2).

✦ Any multiple of 3 can be written as 3n. A multiple of k is written as kn.

What You Need to Show
To prove the result is...Show that the expression...
EvenCan be written as 2 × (something)
OddCan be written as 2 × (something) + 1
Multiple of kCan be written as k × (something) — factorise out k
Always positiveWrite as a perfect square + positive number (e.g. complete the square)
Worked Examples
Prove that the sum of 3 consecutive numbers is always a multiple of 3.
  1. 1
    Write the 3 consecutive numbers:   n,   n+1,   n+2
  2. 2
    Add them:   n + (n+1) + (n+2) = 3n + 3
  3. 3
    Factorise:   3n + 3 = 3(n + 1)
  4. 4
    This is 3 × (n+1), which is a multiple of 3. ✓
Prove that the sum of 3 consecutive even numbers is always a multiple of 6.
  1. 1
    Write the 3 consecutive even numbers:   2n,   2n+2,   2n+4
  2. 2
    Add them:   2n + (2n+2) + (2n+4) = 6n + 6
  3. 3
    Factorise:   6n + 6 = 6(n + 1)
  4. 4
    This is 6 × (n+1), which is a multiple of 6. ✓
Prove that the product of two consecutive odd numbers is always odd.
  1. 1
    Write two consecutive odd numbers:   2n+1   and   2n+3
  2. 2
    Multiply:   (2n+1)(2n+3) = 4n² + 6n + 2n + 3 = 4n² + 8n + 3
  3. 3
    Rewrite:   4n² + 8n + 3 = 2(2n² + 4n + 1) + 1
  4. 4
    This is 2 × (integer) + 1, which is always odd. ✓
